Acute Rheumatic Fever

Jones criteria · strep evidence · echocardiography for carditis · aspirin or prednisone · years of penicillin prophylaxisDid a sore throat come weeks before, and do the findings meet the Jones criteria?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Migratory large-joint arthritis or a new apical holosystolic murmur about 2 to 3 weeks after strep pharyngitis: apply the Jones criteria, which also need evidence of recent group A strep.
  • Order antistreptolysin O and anti-DNase B titers, because the throat swab is often negative by now, and echocardiography for every suspected case.
  • Give penicillin to clear the strep and aspirin for arthritis or mild carditis; then penicillin G benzathine every 3 to 4 weeks for years.
What it is

A nonsuppurative inflammatory complication of group A strep pharyngitis: arthritis, carditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum and chorea.

Bug

Group A strep (Streptococcus pyogenes) pharyngitis, not strep skin infection (impetigo).

Spread

Untreated group A strep pharyngitis (early treatment can prevent rheumatic fever); incidence remains high in resource-poor regions (the family in one NBME stem had lived in a refugee camp).

A prior attack: with untreated strep pharyngitis, recurrence approaches 50%.

Chain

Strep pharyngitis

antibodies to the M protein cross-react with cardiac myosin and basal ganglia antigens (

PathologyAntibodies to strep M protein also bind look-alike self antigens; Aschoff bodies and Anitschkow cells are the pathology findings.

)

valvulitis: mitral regurgitation now

in some, valve stenosis, chiefly mitral, years to decades later

Insights

Valvulitis is the most constant part of carditis: the acute lesion is mitral regurgitation, and mitral stenosis is the late scar.

Chorea can arrive alone, often months after the sore throat, and still meets the criteria once other movement disorders are excluded.

2Urgent risks
Urgent findings
FindingAction
Moderate to severe carditis: cardiomegaly or heart failureGive prednisone instead of aspirin. Severe carditis is the main cause of death in the acute phase.
New strep pharyngitis after a prior attackTreat it promptly and continue prophylaxis; untreated, recurrence approaches 50%.
3Differential
Arthritis or a murmur after an infection
DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Acute rheumatic feverAbout 2 to 3 weeks after strep pharyngitis: migratory large-joint arthritis and a new mitral regurgitation murmur; chorea often months later.Strep titers and echocardiography; count the Jones criteria.
Poststreptococcal reactive arthritisAfter strep, but typically only 1 or 2 joints, less migratory, and slower to respond to aspirin.Order echocardiography to look for carditis.
Lyme diseaseTick exposure and erythema migrans; later arthritis and atrioventricular block, not a new valve murmur.Check for erythema migrans and atrioventricular block; a new valve murmur points away from Lyme.
Fever 5 days or more with nonexudative conjunctivitis, rash, node and hand and foot changes.Count the Kawasaki criteria; the fever comes first, not a sore throat.
Reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome)Arthritis with conjunctivitis and urethritis, often after diarrhea.Check for recent diarrhea or urethritis; it is linked to human leukocyte antigen B27 (HLA-B27).
Arthritis over 6 weeks with no other cause; no strep latency or new murmur.Follow the arthritis beyond 6 weeks and exclude other causes.
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
A camping or travel detail, no tick bite, no rashA setting, not a mechanismCount the Jones criteria and send strep titers.
Abnormal movements months after the sore throatSydenham chorea, enough on its own once other movement disorders are excludedExclude other movement disorders; order echocardiography.
Pause point
Suspected rheumatic fever, negative throat swab Read as excluding rheumatic fever A negative throat swab does not exclude rheumatic fever → Strep titers supply the evidence
5Diagnostic criteria
Jones criteria, first episode
GroupCriteria
Major (JONES)Joints: migratory polyarthritis; O: carditis, clinical or found only on echo; Nodules on extensor surfaces; Erythema marginatum, a fleeting pink rash with sharp edges; Sydenham chorea
MinorFever 38.5 C or higher; polyarthralgia; ESR >60 mm/hour or CRP >30 mg/L; prolonged PR interval
RequiredEvidence of recent group A strep: raised or rising antistreptolysin O or anti-DNase B titer, or a positive culture or rapid test
Rule2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor; chorea alone suffices once other movement disorders are excluded

Polyarthralgia does not count when polyarthritis is the major criterion; a long PR does not count when carditis is.

Carditis sets the treatment
FindingMeaning
Arthritis, no carditis or mild carditisAspirin
Moderate to severe carditis: cardiomegaly or heart failurePrednisone instead of aspirin
Residual valve damage after carditisThe longest prophylaxis (step 8)
7Treatment
1

Clear the strepEvery case

10 days of oral penicillin or amoxicillin, or one injection of penicillin G benzathine.

2

Treat inflammationArthritis or mild carditis

Aspirin; acetaminophen does not treat it.

3

Moderate to severe carditisCardiomegaly or heart failure

Prednisone instead of aspirin; treat the heart failure.

4

Prevent recurrenceAfter the first attack

Penicillin G benzathine IM every 3 to 4 weeks, continued for years (step 8).

8Follow-up
Prophylaxis duration
After the attackContinue for
No carditis5 years or until age 21, whichever is longer
Carditis, no residual heart damage10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer
Carditis with residual heart damageOver 10 years; many experts continue until age 40 or for life
Later
WhenDo
Mitral stenosis years later, symptoms or notStart or continue penicillin prophylaxis.
Dental work with rheumatic valve diseaseNo endocarditis prophylaxis unless a prosthetic valve is present; see .
Chronic rheumatic valve diseaseBe alert for infective endocarditis, a complication of chronic rheumatic heart disease.
Practice
  1. 9 yo M, migratory large-joint arthritis and a new apical holosystolic murmur 2 weeks after pharyngitis → Acute rheumatic fever → penicillin plus anti-inflammatories
  2. 9 yo M with suspected acute rheumatic fever → Anti-streptolysin O titer
  3. 9 yo M with acute rheumatic fever; which valve is most often involved → Mitral
  4. 9 yo M with arthritis 10 days after a diarrheal illness, with conjunctivitis and urethritis → Reactive arthritis
  5. 9 yo M with acute rheumatic fever and new choreiform movements → Sydenham chorea; a major criterion
  6. 9 yo M recovering from acute rheumatic fever → Long-term penicillin prophylaxis
  7. 9 yo M, migratory large-joint arthritis and a new apical holosystolic murmur 2 weeks after pharyngitis; history mentions a recent camping trip → Acute rheumatic fever → the trip is a setting, not a mechanism; no tick bite, no rash, and the latency belongs to the pharyngitis
Mimics Lyme usually brings erythema migrans. Its arthritis is late (months) and usually involves one or a few large joints, and its cardiac finding is AV block (atrioventricular block), not a valvular murmur. RMSF (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) usually brings headache and a rash that spreads to the palms and soles; it is a vasculitis, not an arthritis. JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) needs arthritis beyond 6 weeks by definition.
How NBME framed it No sore throat was mentioned, only a recent refugee camp, which also invited the travel-fever decoys; Kawasaki disease appeared as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, and the mitral murmur was described, not named.
Salient decoyLyme carditis: the camping trip is a setting, not a mechanism; there is no tick bite or erythema migrans, and Lyme gives atrioventricular block, not a new valve murmur.
